title: Escape velocity — the speed that never comes back
intro_sentence: Throw anything upward fast enough and it never falls back — escape velocity is the exact speed at which a body’s kinetic energy just balances the gravity well it is climbing out of.
narrative_101: Gravity never quite lets go — its pull reaches to infinity, only getting weaker with distance. So "escaping" a planet does not mean outrunning gravity; it means having exactly enough energy that, as you climb and slow, you slow toward zero speed only as you reach infinite distance. Come up even a hair short and gravity eventually wins, halts you, and pulls you back. Escape velocity is the knife-edge between those two fates.

From Earth’s surface that speed is about 11.2 kilometres a second — roughly 40,000 km/h. It does not depend on which way you throw the object or how heavy it is: a pebble and a spaceship need the same speed. And it is tied to circular orbital speed by a clean factor — escape velocity is exactly the square root of two (about 1.41) times the speed of a circular orbit at the same height. Reach orbit, then go about 41% faster, and you are gone.

The number that matters for leaving the whole Solar System is bigger: escaping the Sun from Earth’s distance takes about 42 km/s. Earth already carries us around the Sun at about 30, so a probe needs only the difference — but that is still more than most chemical rockets can add on their own, which is why the craft leaving the Solar System leaned on gravity assists: decisive for Voyager and Pioneer, and an added boost for New Horizons, which the biggest launcher of its day had already flung onto an escape trajectory.
body_paragraphs: Escape velocity follows from energy conservation: set total energy (kinetic plus gravitational potential) to zero, and v_escape = √(2μ / r), where μ is the body’s gravitational parameter and r the distance from its centre. Because circular orbital speed is √(μ / r), escape velocity is exactly √2 times it — the same factor at every altitude. A trajectory launched at exactly escape speed is a parabola (orbital energy zero); above it, a hyperbola that arrives at infinity with leftover speed, the "hyperbolic excess" v∞.

The values are worth knowing: ~11.2 km/s from Earth’s surface, ~2.4 km/s from the Moon, ~5.0 km/s from Mars, ~618 km/s from the Sun’s surface, and ~42.1 km/s to escape the Sun from Earth’s 1-AU orbit. Escape speed falls with altitude (larger r), so leaving from a high orbit is cheaper than from the ground — one reason missions build up speed in stages.

Reaching solar escape is why deep-space missions lean on the Oberth effect and gravity assists. Earth’s ~30 km/s orbital motion is a free head start, but the remaining Δv to 42 km/s, applied from low Earth orbit, exceeds a chemical stage’s budget; a planetary flyby donates the rest without propellant. Escape velocity is the target the Physics Lab’s "leave the Solar System" lesson has to clear.
diagram_caption: Escape velocity v = √(2μ/r) = √2 × circular speed: below it the path is a bound ellipse, at it a parabola, above it a hyperbola that reaches infinity with speed to spare.
